description: How plants exchange gases with their surroundings through stomata, lenticels and root surfaces by diffusion, and how these processes change between day and night.

mcq.questionText: The main structures through which gaseous exchange takes place in the leaves are the:
mcq.explanation: Gases enter and leave the leaf through the stomata. Exam Tip: Stomata (mostly lower surface) allow gaseous exchange and transpiration.

mcq.questionText: Each stoma is surrounded by two cells that control its opening and closing, called:
mcq.explanation: A pair of guard cells changes shape to open or close the stoma. Exam Tip: Guard cells are the only leaf-surface cells with chloroplasts.

mcq.questionText: In woody stems, gaseous exchange takes place through small pores in the bark called:
mcq.explanation: Small openings in the bark called lenticels allow gaseous exchange. Exam Tip: Leaves use stomata; woody stems use lenticels; roots use the root surface.

mcq.questionText: During the day, a photosynthesising plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out:
mcq.explanation: By day photosynthesis dominates, so the net gas given out is oxygen. Exam Tip: By day CO2 goes in and O2 comes out because photosynthesis dominates respiration.

mcq.questionText: At night, when there is no photosynthesis, a plant takes in oxygen and gives out:
mcq.explanation: At night only respiration occurs, so oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out. Exam Tip: By night the plant only respires, just like animals.

mcq.questionText: The process by which gases move into and out of the leaf through the stomata is:
mcq.explanation: Gases move down a concentration gradient by diffusion. Exam Tip: Gaseous exchange happens by diffusion, so no energy is needed.

mcq.questionText: Which gas does a plant use during respiration?
mcq.explanation: Oxygen is used to release energy from glucose during respiration. Exam Tip: Plants respire all the time, day and night, using oxygen.

mcq.questionText: Unlike animals, plants do NOT have special breathing organs because:

options.text: Their large surface area and many stomata allow direct diffusion of gases

mcq.explanation: Thin flat leaves with many stomata give a large surface for direct diffusion. Exam Tip: Plants are spread out, so every cell is near air and no lungs are needed.

mcq.questionText: Guard cells open the stomata by:
mcq.explanation: When guard cells gain water and become turgid, they curve apart and the stoma opens. Exam Tip: Turgid means the stoma is open; flaccid means it is closed.

mcq.questionText: Most stomata are found on the lower surface of a leaf. This helps to:

options.text: Reduce water loss while still allowing gaseous exchange

mcq.explanation: The lower surface is cooler and shaded, so placing stomata there reduces evaporation. Exam Tip: Fewer stomata on the hot upper surface means less water is lost.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is TRUE about gaseous exchange and photosynthesis?

options.text: Gaseous exchange supplies and removes the gases used and produced in photosynthesis and respiration
Photosynthesis removes oxygen from the plant

mcq.explanation: Gaseous exchange is the movement of gases, while photosynthesis and respiration are the reactions that use and produce them. Exam Tip: Gaseous exchange is the transport step; photosynthesis and respiration are the reactions.

mcq.questionText: At dawn and dusk, photosynthesis and respiration may occur at equal rates, so no gases are exchanged with the air. This is called the:
mcq.explanation: When the gas made by one process matches the gas used by the other, there is no net exchange, which is the compensation point. Exam Tip: At the compensation point oxygen made equals oxygen used, so no net gas moves.

mcq.questionText: In which part of a plant does gaseous exchange occur through the general surface because there is no waxy cuticle?
mcq.explanation: Gases diffuse directly through the root surface from the air spaces in the soil. Exam Tip: Waterlogged soil has no air and can suffocate roots.

mcq.questionText: Why can waterlogging of soil harm a plant's roots?

options.text: It gives roots too much oxygen
It fills the air spaces with water, so roots cannot get oxygen for respiration

mcq.explanation: Waterlogging fills the soil air spaces with water, cutting off the oxygen supply for root respiration. Exam Tip: Roots respire and need soil air, so waterlogging drowns them.

mcq.questionText: Which one correctly compares gaseous exchange in plants and mammals?

options.text: Plants use stomata and lenticels by diffusion; mammals use lungs (alveoli)

mcq.explanation: Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels by diffusion, while mammals use lungs with alveoli. Exam Tip: Both rely on diffusion across thin moist surfaces, but the structures differ.

fib.questionText: Gaseous exchange in leaves takes place mainly through pores called ____.
fib.explanation: Stomata are the leaf pores through which gases diffuse in and out. Exam Tip: Stomata are mostly on the lower leaf surface.

fib.questionText: Each stoma is opened and closed by two ____ cells.
fib.explanation: A pair of guard cells changes shape to open or close the stoma. Exam Tip: Guard cells contain chloroplasts and change shape with their water content.

fib.questionText: In woody stems, gaseous exchange occurs through pores in the bark called ____.
fib.explanation: Lenticels are the small pores in the bark that allow gaseous exchange. Exam Tip: Lenticels are the woody-stem equivalent of stomata.

fib.questionText: The movement of gases into and out of a leaf occurs by the process of ____.
fib.explanation: Gases move down a concentration gradient, which is diffusion. Exam Tip: Diffusion needs no energy because gases move down a concentration gradient.

fib.questionText: During the day, the gas released by a photosynthesising plant is ____.
fib.explanation: By day photosynthesis dominates, so oxygen is the net gas given out. Exam Tip: By day, photosynthesis dominates, so oxygen is given out.

fib.questionText: At night, a plant carries out only ____, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide.
fib.explanation: At night there is no light, so only respiration takes place. Exam Tip: Respiration happens day and night; at night it is the only gas-exchanging process.

fib.questionText: Guard cells open the stomata when they become ____ (firm with water).
fib.explanation: When guard cells fill with water they become turgid and curve apart, opening the stoma. Exam Tip: Turgid means open; flaccid means closed.

fib.questionText: Gaseous exchange in the roots uses oxygen from the air spaces in the ____.
fib.explanation: Roots take oxygen by diffusion from the air spaces between soil particles. Exam Tip: Waterlogged soil has no air spaces, so roots cannot get oxygen.

fib.questionText: The point at which photosynthesis and respiration occur at equal rates is called the ____ point.
fib.explanation: When the two processes balance, no net gas is exchanged, which defines the compensation point. Exam Tip: At the compensation point there is no net gas exchange.

fib.questionText: In mammals, gaseous exchange takes place in the ____, whereas in plant leaves it takes place through the stomata.
fib.explanation: Mammalian lungs exchange gases across the alveoli, the equivalent of leaf stomata. Exam Tip: Alveoli belong to mammals; stomata and lenticels belong to plants.

tf.questionText: Gaseous exchange in leaves takes place mainly through the stomata.
tf.explanation: The stomata are the main pores for gas movement in leaves. Exam Tip: Stomata serve both gaseous exchange and transpiration.

tf.questionText: Lenticels are found in the leaves of a plant.
tf.explanation: Lenticels are pores in the bark of woody stems, not in leaves. Exam Tip: Lenticels are in the bark of woody stems; leaves use stomata.

tf.questionText: During the day, a plant gives out oxygen as a net gas.
tf.explanation: By day photosynthesis dominates respiration, so oxygen is the net gas released. Exam Tip: Day means net O2 out; night means net CO2 out.

tf.questionText: At night, plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
tf.explanation: At night only respiration occurs, so oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide given out. Exam Tip: At night respiration only means O2 in and CO2 out, the reverse of daytime.

tf.questionText: Gaseous exchange in plants occurs by diffusion.
tf.explanation: Gases move passively down a concentration gradient by diffusion. Exam Tip: No energy is used because diffusion is passive.

tf.questionText: Guard cells close the stomata when they are turgid (full of water).
tf.explanation: Turgid guard cells curve apart and open the stoma; they close it when flaccid. Exam Tip: Turgid means open and flaccid means closed, so this statement is reversed.

tf.questionText: Plants respire both during the day and at night.
tf.explanation: Respiration is continuous, while photosynthesis needs light and stops at night. Exam Tip: Photosynthesis needs light (day only); respiration happens all the time.

tf.questionText: Plants have lungs for gaseous exchange, just like mammals.
tf.explanation: Plants have no lungs; they exchange gases through stomata and lenticels by diffusion. Exam Tip: Plants have no lungs; they use stomata and lenticels by diffusion.

tf.questionText: Waterlogging can kill plant roots by cutting off their oxygen supply.
tf.explanation: Water fills the soil air spaces, so roots cannot get oxygen for respiration. Exam Tip: Roots need oxygen from soil air spaces.

tf.questionText: Both plants and mammals rely on diffusion across thin, moist surfaces for gaseous exchange.
tf.explanation: Despite different structures, both exchange gases by diffusion across thin moist surfaces. Exam Tip: The structures differ, but the diffusion principle is the same.

summary.correctAnswer: Tiny pores, mostly on the lower surface of a leaf, through which gases diffuse in and out.
summary.explanation: Stomata handle both gaseous exchange and transpiration. Exam Tip: Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells.

summary.correctAnswer: A pair of specialised cells surrounding each stoma that open or close it by changing shape.
summary.explanation: They are the only leaf-surface cells with chloroplasts. Exam Tip: When turgid they open the stoma; when flaccid they close it.

summary.correctAnswer: Small pores in the bark of woody stems that allow gaseous exchange.
summary.explanation: They are the woody-stem equivalent of leaf stomata. Exam Tip: Leaves use stomata, woody stems use lenticels.

summary.correctAnswer: The passive movement of gases from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
summary.explanation: It is how gases move in and out of plants. Exam Tip: Diffusion needs no energy because it moves gases down a concentration gradient.

summary.correctAnswer: By day photosynthesis dominates, so the plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen overall.
summary.explanation: Respiration still occurs but is overtaken by photosynthesis. Exam Tip: Day means net oxygen out.

summary.correctAnswer: At night there is no photosynthesis, so the plant only respires, taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide.
summary.explanation: This makes the plant behave like an animal at night. Exam Tip: Night means net carbon dioxide out.

summary.correctAnswer: The point, usually at dawn or dusk, when photosynthesis and respiration occur at equal rates so there is no net gas exchange.
summary.explanation: Oxygen made equals oxygen used, so no net gas moves. Exam Tip: Equal rates mean no net exchange, not both gases released.

summary.correctAnswer: Guard cells that have gained water and become firm, curving apart to open the stoma.
summary.explanation: Loss of water makes them flaccid and closes the stoma. Exam Tip: Turgid means open; flaccid means closed.

summary.questionText: Gaseous exchange in roots and waterlogging
summary.correctAnswer: Roots take in oxygen by diffusion from air spaces in the soil, and waterlogging fills these spaces with water so roots cannot respire.
summary.explanation: The root surface has no waxy cuticle, allowing direct diffusion. Exam Tip: Waterlogged soil drowns roots by removing their air supply.

summary.correctAnswer: Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels by diffusion, while mammals use lungs with alveoli, but both rely on diffusion across thin moist surfaces.
summary.explanation: The principle is the same even though the structures differ. Exam Tip: Compare the structures (stomata versus alveoli), not the diffusion process.

hoq.questionText: A potted plant in a sealed clear box with a carbon dioxide sensor: in BRIGHT LIGHT the carbon dioxide level falls; when covered (DARK) the carbon dioxide rises. Explain both results.

options.text: The plant makes carbon dioxide in light
In light, photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide faster than respiration makes it, so carbon dioxide falls; in the dark, only respiration occurs, releasing carbon dioxide, so it rises
The plant stops respiring in the dark

hoq.explanation: In light photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide faster than respiration makes it, so the carbon dioxide level falls. In the dark only respiration occurs, releasing carbon dioxide, so it rises. Exam Tip: Respiration never stops; in light photosynthesis overtakes it and pulls carbon dioxide down.

hoq.questionText: A student claims plants breathe out only oxygen and never carbon dioxide. Explain why this is wrong.

options.text: The claim is wrong: plants respire at all times, releasing carbon dioxide, and at night (no photosynthesis) they release carbon dioxide overall

hoq.explanation: Plants respire continuously, releasing carbon dioxide. By day photosynthesis uses it and releases oxygen for a net oxygen output, but at night carbon dioxide is released overall. Exam Tip: Only oxygen is just the daytime net result; respiration and its carbon dioxide run constantly.

hoq.questionText: Gaseous exchange at three times: Bright midday (photosynthesis fast, respiration slow); Dawn/dusk (equal rates); Night (no photosynthesis, respiration occurring). Complete the net gas released to air column.
hoq.explanation: At midday photosynthesis exceeds respiration, giving net oxygen. At dawn or dusk rates are equal at the compensation point, so no net gas is released. At night respiration only releases carbon dioxide. Exam Tip: Equal rates mean no net exchange (compensation point), not both gases.
